title: Quantum Probabilistic Local Differential Privacy: Structural Properties and Sample Complexity Bounds
abstract: Differential privacy provides a rigorous framework for quantifying privacy leakage in data analysis, while its quantum extensions have become increasingly relevant with the development of quantum computing and quantum machine learning. In this work, we introduce and study quantum probabilistic local differential privacy, a relaxation of quantum local differential privacy in which the privacy constraint is allowed to fail on a spectral violation event with low probability. This quantity can be interpreted as the probability under the quantum superoperation of a quantum privacy-loss violation, and is closely related to the acceptance probability of the quantum Neyman-Pearson test at a small threshold. We investigate the basic structural properties of this privacy notion and clarify its relationship with existing forms of quantum differential privacy. We show the properties of quantum probabilistic local differential privacy under tensor-product composition and unitary post-processing, while it is in general neither convex nor closed under post-processing by arbitrary quantum channels. We further characterize when depolarizing noise satisfies quantum probabilistic local differential privacy under several representative scenarios. Finally, we connect quantum probabilistic privacy constraints with statistical inference by deriving a lower bound on probabilistically privatized contraction coefficients in terms of the hockey-stick divergence. As an application, we obtain sample complexity bounds of probabilistically privated asymmetric and symmetric quantum hypothesis testing. These results provide a systematic foundation for studying probabilistic privacy guarantees in quantum information processing and their operational consequences for private quantum statistical inference.
summary: This paper establishes Quantum Probabilistic Local Differential Privacy (QPrLDP) as a relaxed framework for quantifying privacy loss in quantum data analysis. It analyzes the structural properties of this notion and applies it to derive concrete sample complexity bounds for private quantum hypothesis testing. This provides essential theoretical tools for ensuring privacy guarantees when performing statistical inference using quantum resources.
main_problem: The paper introduces and rigorously studies Quantum Probabilistic Local Differential Privacy (QPrLDP), a relaxation of quantum local differential privacy.
main_result: It derives sample complexity bounds for probabilistically privatized asymmetric and symmetric quantum hypothesis testing, providing a systematic foundation for probabilistic privacy guarantees in quantum inference.
method: The study involves defining QPrLDP based on spectral violation probabilities and connecting it to statistical inference via the hockey-stick divergence. Structural properties are analyzed using tensor products and unitary post-processing.
model_or_system: The analysis is conducted within the framework of quantum information processing, involving quantum states ($ho, \sigma$), superoperators (channels), and measurements characterized by POVMs. The context includes depolarizing noise models.
key_observables: Trace distance $T(ho||\sigma)$, Quantum hockey-stick divergence $	ext{E}_\gamma(ho||\sigma)$, Sample complexity measures ($	ext{SC}, 	ext{ASC}$), and error probabilities ($\alpha,  eta$).
important_parameters: Privacy parameters $(\epsilon, \delta)$ and the noise parameter $p$ (for depolarizing noise).
main_assumptions: The work builds upon existing concepts of classical and quantum differential privacy, QLDP, and various quantum divergences.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the relationship between $\delta$ and $\epsilon$ for global depolarizing noise, showing how $\delta$ scales with the number of compositions ($n$).
paper_structure: The paper systematically defines QPrLDP, investigates its structural properties (composition, post-processing), characterizes specific noise models (depolarizing noise), and culminates in deriving explicit lower and upper bounds for sample complexity in quantum hypothesis testing.
why_interesting: While focused on privacy theory, the rigorous mathematical tools developed—especially those involving divergences and channel analysis—are highly relevant to characterizing information leakage or distinguishability in open quantum systems.
